newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arafat seeks more aid from World Bank donors.
newsitem.headline: Arafat seeks more aid from World Bank donors.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat lobbied World Bank donors on Wednesday in a drive to boost aid for the West Bank and Gaza at a time of severe economic strain in the autonomous Palestinian areas.

The Bank's Consultative Group, which was meeting in Paris, has so far pledged some $2.9 billion in assistance to the areas for 1994-98, but Palestinian leaders are keen to ensure that pledges are fulfilled.
Arafat worked his way around the conference table, embracing many of the representatives from some 40 countries and international organisations before delivering a speech behind closed doors.

The Palestinian president, who will meet French Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette later on Wednesday, will hold a news conference at 1630 GMT after the World Bank meeting called to solicit pledges for aid for World Bank programmes in 1997.

Israel's decision to close off the West Bank and Gaza in February after a wave of bomb attacks by Moslem fundamentalists killed dozens of people in Israel has weighed heavily on the economy of both areas.
According to the World Bank, the political situation has resulted in projections of a five percent decline of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for 1996 in the autonomous Palestinian areas.

A main hope for improvement is the expected opening in about two months of the al-Muntar industrial park on the Palestinian side of the Israel-Gaza Strip border, World Bank officials said ahead of the meeting.
Under the best conditions, the project will employ 17,000 people directly, mostly in textiles, and 35,000 indirectly by early 1998.
Kemal Dervis, World Bank vice-president for the Middle East and North Africa, said that barring new political upheavals "there is no reason that the Palestinian economy cannot do well".

"The bad situation is due to political and security constraints as well as uncertainty in the minds of potential investors. But this is not a situation that is so bad it cannot work. Things can and do advance," he said.
Referring to Israel's past sudden closures of Palestinian areas following terror attacks, Dervis said rules can be set to allow for trading while respecting Israel's security concerns.

A meeting on economic assistance to the Palestinians in Paris in January made pledges totalling $856 million. World Bank documents showed that at the end of August, commitments stood at $559 million and disbursements at $287 million.
